                B.​ Penal Code Section 496(c) is Governed by a One-Year Statute of Limitations.
 3

 4   ​       Section 340(a) of the California Code of Civil Procedure provides a one-year limitations

 5   period for “an action upon a statute for a penalty or forfeiture.” C.C.P. § 340(a). The courts have

 6   recognized that Penal Code § 496(c) is a penal statute, and the statute authorizes treble damages

 7   and fees to a private plaintiff injured by theft. California and federal courts applying California

 8   law hold that statutes providing double or treble damages are “penal” in nature and subject to the

 9   one-year statute of limitations found in CCP § 340(a). See Le v. Prestige Cmty. Credit Union,

10   2023 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 232717, at *25 (citing Prudential Home Mortg. Co., 66 Cal. App. 4th at

11   1242). In Prudential Home Mortg., the California Court of Appeals evaluated the following

12   three factors to determine whether sums imposed under a statute constituted a penalty or

13   forfeiture governed by the one-year statute of limitations, or whether they were remedial and

14   governed by a longer limitations period: (1) whether the statute’s language characterizes the

15   sums as a penalty or forfeiture, (2) whether the legislative history refers to the sums as a penalty

16   or forfeiture, and (3) whether the sums are imposed without reference to the actual damage

17   sustained by the plaintiff.

18           Here, all three factors weigh in favor of finding that Jefferies’s Third Claim for relief

19   under Penal Code § 496(c) is subject to a one-year statute of limitations. Section 496(c) is found

20   in the Penal Code and requires underlying proof of buying or receiving stolen property, which is

21   a crime defined under subsection (a). The amendments and legislative history in the notes to the

22   statute show that it has always been a Penal Code enactment. See Penal Code § 496,

23   amendments. The enhanced penalties of treble damages, costs of suit, and reasonable attorney’s

24   fees under subsection (c) are fixed, do not vary on a sliding scale, and are imposed without

25   reference to the amount of damages sustained by the plaintiff. See Los Angeles Unified School

26   Dist. v. Superior Court, 14 Cal.5th 758, 778 (2023) (“This court and others have frequently

27   characterized treble damages as exemplary or punitive.”).
